The Plumbeous seedeater (Sporophila plumbea) initiates breeding during the austral spring, when females typically produce clutches of two eggs [N_R_i = clutches of two eggs]. Field observations indicate that reproductive activity is sustained under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of the breeding season, at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], where individuals may attempt more than one nesting event annually, with a recorded frequency of about 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 1.5 clutches per year]. The eggs themselves are small, and upon being laid, a freshly deposited ovum has an initial wet weight of 1.55 grams [Ww0 = 1.55 grams], a modest mass that reflects the limited maternal investment per offspring typical of many small-bodied Neotropical passerines. This initial measurement is consistent with the broader reproductive strategy of the species, which balances low per-offspring investment against the potential for multiple broods within a single favorable season, especially when food resources are abundant.

Incubation of the embryonated eggs occurs over a precise developmental period, with hatching taking place after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] when the nest is maintained at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This incubation duration is typical for a passerine of this body size and reflects the efficient thermal transfer provided by the brooding adult. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling is notably underdeveloped, and its wet weight at birth is only 1.2 grams [Wwb = 1.2 grams]. This neonatal mass, among the lowest recorded for thraupid finches, underscores the extreme altriciality of the chicks and their heavy dependence on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The yolk reserves absorbed during late incubation are rapidly exhausted, necessitating the prompt onset of exogenous feeding by both parents to support the chick's subsequent growth trajectory.

During the nestling stage, the developing chick experiences a period of rapid mass gain as it is fed a diet of seeds and insects by both parents. Under the sustained warm conditions typical of the breeding environment, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the fledging event—marked by the achievement of first flight and nest departure—occurs at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period for a finch of this size. This accelerated development is likely an adaptive response to high nest predation pressure in its grassland and scrubland habitats. Following fledging, the juvenile bird remains dependent on parental care for several additional weeks, during which its flight feathers continue to mature and its foraging skills improve. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females, which represents the asymptotic mass of the species, has been recorded at 10.3 grams [Wwi = 10.3 grams], a value that places S. plumbea among the smaller members of the genus Sporophila.

Sexual maturation in the Plumbeous seedeater follows a predictable schedule under the thermal conditions typical of its active life phase, near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of adult plumage characteristics in males, is reached at 36 days since birth [tp = 36 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid maturation from hatching to reproductive viability is characteristic of many opportunistic tropical and subtropical passerines that must capitalize on brief windows of resource abundance. The first reproduction event, however, is typically deferred until the following breeding season; the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between achieving physiological maturity and initiating reproductive effort is widespread among small Neotropical finches and likely reflects the time required for young birds to establish territories, acquire sufficient body condition, and gain the experience necessary for successful nesting.

The maximum lifespan of the Plumbeous seedeater in natural populations has been estimated from long-term banding studies to be about 6 years [am = about 6 years] under the warm environmental conditions characteristic of its range, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity, while modest compared to some larger-bodied passerines, is substantial for a bird with a female adult mass of only 10.3 grams [Wwi = 10.3 grams] and suggests that adult mortality rates in the wild are relatively low once individuals have survived their vulnerable first year. Comparative analyses with congeneric species, such as the Lined seedeater (Sporophila lineola), reveal that while S. plumbea has a slightly shorter lifespan, it compensates through a higher annual reproductive output. The species also exhibits a degree of site fidelity, with banded adults often returning to the same breeding territories across consecutive seasons, a behavioral trait that may enhance individual survival by familiarizing birds with local food sources and predator escape routes.
